children: by Randall W. Forsyth

A quarter-century ago, our world changed. The terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center and Pentagon shattered America's sense that nothing could dent its security or station in the world. From an economic standpoint, the nation's fiscal status has been turned upside down-from a federal budget swimming in surpluses to one deeply in deficit, despite the U.S. not being in recession or officially at war.

Since then, the world has become even more dangerous, with the Iran war, Russia's war on Ukraine, and China's adventures in the Pacific. At the same time, the U.S. has grown financially weaker by many measures. We're now spending more on interest than on the military. In short, we're approaching next Friday's 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in distinctly ominous circumstances.

The Up & Down Wall Street written directly after the 9/11 attacks predicted a marked increase in spending for national security. I remember that because that column happened to be the first Up & Down Wall Street assigned to me. Alan Abelson, the originator and longtime writer of the column, had earlier asked me to fill in while he took a rare, well-deserved vacation. Neither of us could imagine what would transpire while he was away.

"The Peace Dividend has been eliminated," I began.   We would need to spend much more on security, which would divert resources from investments that would pay off in greater wealth and well-being at home. The relative peace following the end of the Cold War, now shattered, had helped to bring prosperity at the close of the 20th century. The toppling of the Twin Towers provided a counterpoint to the fall of the Berlin Wall.

Some 15 years later, evidence of that hypothesis emerged. As I wrote then, a recently published tome, The Political Economy of Terrorism, from two academics, concluded that homeland security spending siphoned off private capital and slowed overall growth. To be sure, those resources weren't wasted-many attacks were thwarted post-9/11.

What couldn't be imagined is the extent to which the debts of governments, not just Washington but globally, have been pushed so deeply into the red. That can't entirely be laid to the rising cost of military expenditure, although the tab for the subsequent wars in Iraq and Afghanistan importantly figure in turning surpluses into deficits.

Nor could we anticipate the financial crisis of 2008-09 and the Covid pandemic. But clearly on the horizon at the time was the demographic certainty of the retirement of the baby boomers, which now is set to deplete the Social Security retirement trust fund by 2032.

Before 9/11, the fall of the Soviet Union helped pare military spending as a share of the federal budget, noted David Kelly, J.P. Morgan Asset Management's chief global strategist. There was also a strong political push toward reducing budget deficits in the 1990s, starting with President George H.W. Bush's tax hikes that abrogated his "Read my lips, no new taxes" pledge, helping to scuttle his re-election in 1992. President Bill Clinton's tax hikes and spending restraint after Republicans captured both houses of Congress in 1994 combined with the technology and stock market booms of the decade to further help push the budget into the black.

That all changed after the turn of the century. Vice President Dick Cheney declared, "Reagan proved that deficits don't matter." So, since 2000, publicly held debt zoomed from $3.4 trillion to $32 trillion, Kelly continued, in part reflecting tax cuts in 2001, 2017, and 2025. Those reduced federal revenue to 16.7% of gross domestic product from 19.1% in 2000, Kelly wrote in a client note. Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid rose to 10.1% of GDP from 7.8% while other expenditures (excluding interest) increased to 5.6% of GDP from 4.5%.

Military spending's increase over that span was relatively contained, to 4.4% from 3.5% of GDP. But the Office of Management and Budget is now seeking a massive 43% increase in military expenditure, to over $1.5 trillion, for fiscal 2027, which begins on Oct. 1. That request comes amid reports that munitions have been depleted by the Iran war.

Congress is unlikely to go along with the administration's big ask, according to Capital Alpha Partners Washington analyst Byron Callan. His "worst case" scenario is for a fiscal-2027 continuing resolution with $903 billion in military outlays plus $72 billion in supplemental spending for defense and intelligence.

What's clear is that bond yields have risen around the globe since the start of the Iran war at the end of February, says Doug Peta, who heads BCA's Essentials Team. Much of that reflects not just the jump in petroleum prices but also the even greater surge in refined products, especially diesel fuel, which is an important input in the price of moving nearly everything.

What's also clear is that the increase in military spending is global, not just in Washington, Peta writes in a research report: "As the U.S. dials back its role as the principal guarantor of the postwar order, the potential for military conflicts around the world has risen. In the new multipolar world order, individual states have a greater need to provide for their own defense and will rejigger their budget priorities to obtain the weapons systems required to secure it."

Total global military spending as a percentage of world GDP has already climbed to nearly 2.5% from under 2.2% in 2022, according to BCA's numbers. In the European Union, military spending is projected to rise proportionally more, to 1.9% of GDP from 1.5%. Japan's military outlays are up to over 1.3% of GDP from about 1.0%.

An end to the Ukraine and Iran wars will only temporarily slow military spending growth, he continues. Tensions in Europe will remain high, with "Russia posing a material threat to NATO and former Warsaw Pact states." Iran's ability and willingness to menace the Persian Gulf states will mean the need for missile defense systems and other weapons, he adds.

In the U.S., even a Democratic capture of both the House of Representatives and the Senate (a 60% chance, according to BCA geopolitical strategists, but only a coin toss, according to prediction markets) wouldn't pull the plug on military appropriations, given the drawdown of weapons stocks in Iran that have to be replenished. All of which hasn't gone unnoticed by defense and aerospace stocks, which actually may have gotten ahead of themselves, he concludes.
What's different from 25 years ago is that the U.S. now faces this dangerous world deeply in debt.

These high and persistent budget deficits have boosted bond yields around the globe to such an extent that they have entered the zeitgeist-they even made it to Page One of the New York Times this past week. That came as the U.S. Treasury 10-year note yield hit its highest level since 2023, while the German counterpart rose to its highest level since 2011.

Elsewhere, French government yields reached their highest point since 2008, while United Kingdom gilt yields rose to their highs since 2007. Budget and spending issues are big political issues in those countries, as well. In France, a likely far-left candidate in next year's elections has floated a "burn the bonds" scheme to deal with the debt in which the central bank would cancel its holdings of French government obligations. That's a reflection of how budget battles are becoming political instead of just economic.

Nor is it just government issuance; massive corporate borrowing to finance artificial-intelligence projects is also driving up interest rates. The debt issuance by the five hyperscalers (Amazon.com, Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta Platforms, and Oracle), Nvidia, and special purpose vehicles to finance AI totals about $320 billion so far this year, writes Michael Cembalest, chairman of market and investment strategy for J.P. Morgan Asset Management, in a client note. The long-duration component amounts to $310 billion, he estimates, equal to 50% of Treasury long-duration issuance this year.

The debt Cassandras have been sounding alarms about government debt since the Reagan years. Economists from Morgan Stanley call the latest headlines "A 40 Trillion Dollar Distraction," arguing that the Congressional Budget Office's long-term expectation of a 10-year Treasury yield of 4.4% is a full percentage point too high. Similarly, in D.C., debt concerns elicit just shrugs, the New York Times reported.

But Robin J. Brooks, the former head of Goldman Sachs' currency group, now at the Brooking Institute, has been all over the international bond debacle. He contends that the U.S. debt situation is worse than it appears, which is why Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent made his surprise bond buyback announcement a few weeks ago, Brooks maintains.

Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh talked tough on inflation at Jackson Hole a week ago, a reversal from his dovish talk after the July 29 policy meeting, which sent bonds up sharply. "In my opinion, there's a new Treasury-Fed accord taking shape, where the main goal is to keep longer-term yields contained in the face of out-of-control deficits," Brooks wrote in his Substack post.

That takes on greater importance with the U.S. government already spending over $1 trillion annually on interest, more than on the military. Paying more to service the debt than for the military has meant the demise of past great powers, as economic historian Niall Ferguson has said.

"Absent some dramatic political change, investors should expect that the federal government will go broke slowly," J.P. Morgan's Kelly advises. "However, they should be prepared in case some exogenous force or even greater political irresponsibility causes a slow deterioration to turn into a free fall," he dolefully concludes.

The events of 9/11 marked a turning point in geopolitics and public finances. Now we face an even more dangerous world with less wherewithal to deal with it. Let's hope the Cassandras are still wrong.
